topics.T2: A confrontation that crosses physical lines

excerpts.text:
She locked the door. He sat on the bed. The light was bad. She did not switch it on.

She took off her shirt. He watched. She took off her jeans. The fan turned in the corner.

"Come here," she said.

He came. She undid his belt. The buckle clicked twice. His mouth tasted of gin. Her hands were cold.

He pulled her down. The mattress was old. The springs gave. She laughed against his neck.

She moved on top of him. His hands went up her ribs. She did not speak. He did not speak. The fan turned.

She bit his shoulder. He gripped her hip. The bed knocked the wall once. She did not slow down.

He came first. She kept going. He held her by the small of the back. She closed her eyes. She finished. The room was quiet again.

She lay on her side. He lay on his. The fan turned. The light from the window was blue.

"Cigarette," she said.

He got up. The floor was cold. He brought the pack and the lighter and a glass of water. She took the glass first. She drank half of it. She handed it back.

He lit the cigarette and gave it to her. She held it up. Smoke went sideways. The room smelled like sweat and old beer and tobacco. She did not mind.

"Stay," she said.

"All right."

He lay down again. The mattress complained. She put her hand on his stomach and left it there. She finished the cigarette. He took it from her and crushed it in a saucer on the floor.

She slept first. He listened to the fan. He did not sleep for a long time.

Marek stood in the doorway. He did not come in.

"You have something of mine," he said.

Karol was at the table. He had a coffee. He did not get up.

"Sit down."

"No."

"Suit yourself."

Marek shut the door behind him. The room was small. A kettle on the stove. A coat on a hook. Nothing else.

"The papers," Marek said.

"I do not have them."

"You have them."

"I had them. I gave them to Andrzej."

"You are lying."

Karol drank his coffee. He set the cup down. He looked at the door.

"I am not lying."

Marek walked to the table. He put both hands on it. The wood was thin. The table moved a little.

"You will get them back from him."

"I cannot."

"You will."

"He is in Gdansk."

"Then go to Gdansk."

Karol did not answer. Marek waited. The kettle made a sound. Not boiling. Just settling on the cold burner.

"Tomorrow," Marek said.

"All right."

"Tonight."

"It is the train. It does not run after ten."

"There is a bus."

Karol stood up. He was a head shorter than Marek. He did not step back.

"I will go tomorrow."

"Tonight."

Marek did not move. Karol did not move. Then Karol's hand went to the back of his belt. Marek saw it. He saw it before the hand stopped.

He hit Karol once. The cup went off the table. It did not break. Karol went down. He sat on the floor and held his jaw.

Marek picked up the coffee cup. He set it on the table.

"Tonight," he said.

He let himself out. The door clicked. Karol did not get up for a long time.

He woke at six. The flat was cold. He stayed under the blanket. Outside, a tram on the wet street.

He got up. He pulled on yesterday's trousers. He looked for his shirt and did not find it. He took a clean one from the chair.

In the kitchen the kettle was already warm. She had been up. Her cup was in the sink. Coffee, not tea. The grounds were wet.

A note on the table. Two lines.

Going to Father. Back Sunday.

He read it twice. He read it again. He folded it and put it in his pocket.

He made coffee. He drank it standing. The window faced the courtyard. The pigeons were on the rail.

He took her cup out of the sink and washed it. He dried it. He put it back on the shelf next to his own.

The phone rang. He did not answer it. The phone stopped.

He sat at the table. He drank the rest of the coffee. It went cold before he finished it.

At eight he put on his coat. He locked the door. He went down the stairs. The neighbour's dog barked once. He did not stop.

On the street it was raining. He stood under the awning of the bakery. He bought a roll. He ate half of it and threw the rest to the pigeons.

He walked to the office. He was not late. He sat at his desk. He worked.

At lunch he went out and called her sister.

"She is here," her sister said.

"Good."

"She said do not come."

"All right."

He hung up. He went back to the office. He worked until seven. Then he went home and ate bread and slept early. The flat was still cold.

He brought her to the bed under the high window where the rain was running silver down the panes and the lamps below in the courtyard threw a wandering amber against the ceiling, and she stood while he undressed her piece by piece as a man stripping the layers of some sacred and forbidden book, the lacework of her stays loosed and falling, the chemise lifted over the crown of her hair, the hem of her shift drawn away from the long pale arch of her flank, and the air that touched her was cold and smelt of the wet stones of the city and the sea beyond.

He pressed his mouth to the small hollow at the base of her throat where the pulse moved like something interred and beating against an oaken door, and his hand went down across the bone of her hip and the cleft of her thigh, and she breathed out a sound that was neither word nor cry but the older language of the body, ancient and unholy, common to all that walks and rouses and dies.

She drew him down upon her in the dim wash of the lamp, and he came to her hungering as a man come at last to the table of his oldest sin, and she opened beneath him and took him into her warmth like an offering received by the priestess of an old religion, and she said nothing but the breath of him close at her ear, and the sheets tangled at their feet like a shroud cast off, and the rain ran down the high glass and the amber light wandered the ceiling and the bed groaned beneath them as a ship beneath an old and patient labour.

After, he lay across her like a man fallen, and she held him there with her fingers in the wet of his hair, and the lamps in the courtyard guttered and the rain went on.

She came down the corridor with the candle held before her in her cupped hand and the wax running slow over her knuckles, and she found him in the long room where the curtains hung black and heavy as the vestments of some old order of mourning, and he turned at the sound of her step.

"You ought not be here," he said.

She did not answer. She set the candle upon the table where the silver was cold and tarnished from a hundred dinners no longer eaten, and she crossed to him over the dark Persian carpet that had been her grandmother's and her grandmother's before that, and the bone of her shoulder caught the light as a pale slip of moon between cloud.

He took her by the wrist when she came near and his grip was the grip of a man who has decided long since that he will not be moved, and she did not pull from him but only held his eyes with her own and the room about them grew hushed as the room of a chapel at the moment between a question and a vow.

"You ought not be here," he said again.

"I have come."

He drew her against him then with a violence that was the violence of long restraint at last unfastened, and he set his mouth to the hollow at the corner of her jaw and his teeth grazed the skin and she shut her eyes and her hand at his collar closed and would not loose, and outside in the corridors the wind moved through the house as a thing seeking its lost rest, and the candle on the table burned low and the wax pooled black in the plate, and neither of them spoke.

She would not afterward remember which of them had been the first to bring the other to the floor.

The morning came in slow upon the high window where the curtains hung half-drawn and the light fell across the bed in long stripes the colour of old gold, and she lay upon her side with her hair undone and her cheek against the bare hollow of his shoulder, and he was already half awake and watching the dust turn in the air.

She did not speak for a long while. There was a smell in the room of the wax of the burnt-down candles and the salt of bodies and the old wet wool of his coat where he had dropped it upon the chair by the door, and somewhere far below in the kitchens of the house a girl was singing some lament her mother had taught her, and the words could not be made out but the slow falling cadence of them came up through the floors as through deep water.

He set his palm flat to the small of her back and held it there, and she felt the heat of him and she felt also the slow grief which had attended them both these last hours and had not gone away, only abated, only lain down with them in the dark and risen again in the morning beside them.

She thought to speak. She did not. To name a thing was to call it. The room smelt of the candle and of him and of the rain on the slates, and she let it be.

After a time he kissed the crown of her hair where it lay tangled against the pillow, and he rose and dressed without speaking, and she watched him at the mirror buttoning his shirt as if he were a stranger come into her chamber from another house and another year. He drew the curtain wider. The light was longer than it had been. She closed her eyes.

She let him in without saying anything, just stood back from the door, and he came in and put his coat on the radiator, the way he always did, like he lived here, which he didn't. She thought, he didn't. She thought she should say something. She didn't.

He turned and looked at her and she felt, for a moment, almost embarrassed, as if she had been caught at something, although there was nothing to catch her at; she had only been waiting for him. Or she had been waiting for him for half an hour and reading a book about, what, French art criticism, and trying not to listen for the buzzer. Both at once.

He said, hi. She said, hi. They were still standing in the hallway.

Later, on the bed, with the lamp off and the streetlight coming in cold across the duvet, she thought about how this had become familiar, how the shape of him over her was a shape she now knew, and she did not know what to do with knowing it. Was it a comfort or was it the slow shutting of a door. She did not know. He was kissing her throat and she let him and she did not know.

It was not bad. It was the opposite of bad. That was not the problem. The problem was, she could not tell if she was here, in this bed, with him, doing this — or if she was watching herself do it. She thought: this is the thing they mean. When they say it. About being twenty-six.

She put her hand in his hair and pulled, a little, the way he liked, and she heard him make a sound, and she thought, good. Then she thought, that is a strange thing to think. Then she stopped thinking, which was, she supposed, the point of it. For a while.

After, he said her name. She said, mm. It was enough.

She had told him not to come. She had said it on the phone and again in the email, and she had thought, that is two times, that is enough, and then he came anyway.

He stood in the doorway of the office and she felt — she did not know what she felt. Tired? She felt tired. Also: she felt watched, by the others, the four other people at four other desks, all of whom had heard her on the phone, three weeks ago, saying his name like that. She thought: please go.

"Five minutes," he said.

She got up. They went into the kitchen because the kitchen was empty. She closed the door and then thought, why did I close the door. Closing the door looked like, she did not know, intimacy. Concealment. Something.

"You said five minutes."

"I know what I said."

He stepped closer than he should have, and she did not step back, which she should have done, which she would later, lying in bed at home, think about not having done. Why hadn't she. She did not know. She knew. She knew and she did not want to know.

He put his hand on the side of her face. Not hard. The way he used to, in the bad weeks. She thought, oh. She thought, this is — this. She thought several things in a small narrow row.

Her body, which seemed lately to have its own ideas, tipped slightly toward him. Like a plant in a window. She heard herself breathing.

She said, stop.

She was not sure she had said it. She said it again.

He took his hand away. He stepped back. He was, suddenly, just a man in a doorway again, and she thought, oh, that is how easy it was, all along.

She did not say anything else. She opened the door and waited. He left. She stood in the kitchen and made tea she did not drink.

She woke up before the alarm, which surprised her — usually she slept right through it — and lay still for a while because moving would mean moving, would mean the day, would mean putting on the dressing gown which was on the back of the door and which she would have to cross the cold floor to reach, and instead she just lay there looking at the ceiling.

The ceiling had a damp patch in the corner. She had been meaning to email the landlord about it for weeks. She thought: I will email him today. She thought: probably I will not.

He had gone, she could tell, without listening for him, just by the quiet — the flat sounded the way it sounded when she was alone in it, which had a particular shape to it, a thinness, like a kettle that had stopped whistling. She did not mind. They had agreed about this. He had work, she had work, he had said something last night about a train at six. She thought: was that last night or the night before. She could not quite remember. The week had run into itself in the way weeks did now, in her late twenties, when nothing in particular had happened to fix one day apart from another.

She made herself get up. The dressing gown. The kettle. She stood at the window with her hands around the cup and watched a man across the road walking a small black dog. The dog was doing something exuberant with a leaf.

She thought: it had been nice. Last night. It had been nice in a way that, she thought, neither of them had quite expected. She felt something move in her chest, not quite happiness, more like the way you felt when a difficult sentence finally landed. Then she finished her tea and went to look for her trousers.

0023. Hotel Continental, Room 814. Subject Two-One entered at 2358 with the asset; door secured 0001; ambient surveillance dark per protocol Black-Six.

Two-One moved to the bed. The asset stood by the desk and removed her coat. She placed it across the back of the chair, sleeves down, collar even. She did not speak.

Two-One sat. He removed his jacket and folded it on the bedside table. He kept his sidearm in the shoulder rig. The asset noted this and made no comment.

She walked across. She placed both hands on his shoulders. She straddled him. Her weight was approximately fifty-eight kilos, distributed forward on the knees.

Two-One disengaged the rig and set it on the table at arm's reach. He unbuttoned her blouse from the collar down, four buttons. He paused at the fifth and watched her face. She nodded once. He continued.

Subsequent contact, eighteen minutes, conventional. Heart rate elevated, normal range for activity. No vocalisation above baseline. The mattress mechanism was silent. The wall to Room 813 was double-skinned and rated.

At 0019 the asset shifted. Two-One let her. She moved on top of him. Position maintained for nine minutes. Two-One disengaged at 0028, ten seconds before climax; the asset finished above, hand braced on his sternum, head turned away from the door.

She moved off him. She walked to the bathroom. She drank water from the tap. She returned. She lay on the side of the bed nearest the window.

Two-One re-engaged the rig before he lay down. Standard. He set the sidearm on the table within reach.

The asset said: "You always do that."

Two-One said: "Yes."

She turned to face the window. He listened to her breathing for thirty seconds and noted it slowing. He reached over and switched off the lamp. The room went to ambient amber from the street. He did not sleep.

0712. Warehouse 4, dock side, north bay. Pavlenko stood inside the rolling door with his hands visible. Reyes stood three paces inside the line, sidearm holstered, badge folded in the breast pocket.

"You are early," Pavlenko said.

"You are alone," Reyes said. "That is the wrong way around."

"My driver is outside."

"Your driver left twelve minutes ago. We have the plate."

Pavlenko's hands moved fractionally — wrist tendon, no further. Reyes catalogued it and waited.

"You wanted to talk," Pavlenko said.

"I wanted the manifest."

"There is no manifest."

"There is always a manifest."

Pavlenko stepped forward. One pace. Reyes did not move.

"Stop there," Reyes said.

Pavlenko did not stop. Reyes drew, low ready, and the action took approximately one-point-two seconds from holster to muzzle on target. Pavlenko stopped.

"Hands on the wall."

"Reyes —"

"Hands. Wall. Step back. Now."

Pavlenko stepped back. He did not put his hands on the wall. Reyes closed the gap to within striking distance and made the decision in the half-second before Pavlenko's right shoulder rotated — preemptive contact, open palm, base of the jaw. Pavlenko went down hard onto one knee. Reyes kept the sidearm muzzled at the floor, his off-hand bracing Pavlenko's collar.

"Stay down."

Pavlenko stayed down.

Reyes secured the cuffs left-handed, off-hand kept on the collar, sidearm re-holstered at the four-second mark. Total time, from drawn to cuffed: eight seconds. Within tolerance.

"Walk," Reyes said.

Pavlenko walked. They moved through the rolling door into the lot. The second unit was already in position at the perimeter and Reyes raised one hand to acknowledge them, and Garcia stepped out from behind the second unit with the bag for the manifest, which Reyes had not yet found, and which Pavlenko did not yet know they would find inside his coat lining, second pocket, left-side.

0612. Hotel Continental, Room 814.

Two-One woke at the standard wake-tick. He confirmed the asset still in position on the window side of the bed, breathing regular, pulse confirmed visually at the throat at approximately fifty-eight. He confirmed sidearm in rig, table to his right, untouched.

He moved to the bathroom. Standard hygiene sequence, four minutes. He returned dressed in slacks and undershirt. The asset was awake. She had not moved.

"Coffee," she said.

"Room service is logged. Negative."

"Then the kettle."

He used the kettle. He produced two cups. He gave her one and kept one.

She sat up. She wrapped the sheet around herself. The mark on her neck — left clavicle, approximately four centimetres lateral of the sternal notch — was faint. He noted it without comment. Five days, he estimated. Probably less.

"You will be at the embassy at ten," he said.

"I know."

"You will say you were here."

"I know."

"You will say it was uneventful."

"I know what to say."

He drank his coffee. She drank hers. Neither hurried.

After two minutes she said: "Last night."

"Yes."

"That cannot happen again."

"No."

She held the cup in both hands and looked toward the window. The curtains were drawn but the light around the edges was getting lighter. She said:

"It was a mistake."

"Operationally?"

"Operationally."

"Yes."

"Personally also."

He did not answer. He finished his coffee and set the cup down precisely on the cork coaster on the bedside table. He picked up the rig and put it on. He buttoned his shirt over it. He took his jacket from the chair.

At the door he paused.

"It will not be in the report," he said.

"No."

He let himself out. The corridor was empty. He took the service stairs.

queries.text:
The room had two beds. She did not look at the second one. She closed the door and turned the key.

"You drink anything?" he said.

"No."

He did not either. He sat on the bed. She took off her boots. She put them under the chair. She came across.

She stood between his knees. He looked up. She did not say anything. She did not have to.

He pulled her down. The bed was narrow. They did not use the second one.

She bit his lip once. He held her by the back of the neck. She liked that. He knew that. The lamp by the bed was on. She did not switch it off.

He turned her onto her back. She let him. He was heavier than she remembered. That was all right. She moved her hips up to meet him.

Outside, a truck on the highway. Once. Then nothing. The window was open a finger's width. The curtain did not move. The room was hot.

She said his name once, low.

She came across the courtyard in the falling light with the lamp held low at her side and the smoke of the rain rising about her ankles, and she saw him standing in the open doorway of the carriage house against the dim red of the forge fire within. He did not move toward her. He waited as a man waits for a sentence to be passed, and the wet stones of the yard shone beneath her feet like the faces of a thousand small mute saints, and she stopped before him at the threshold and the rain came in past her shoulder and fell upon his bare arm where the muscle was wet and lit.

"You were not to come," he said.

"I have come."

He took the lamp from her hand and set it upon the anvil where the iron lay cooling, and he turned back and his eyes were on her in a manner that had in it the long contained heat of the forge itself, and the air about them was charged as the air of a chamber before storm, and she did not move but only stood and let him —

He was already there when she got back from the corner shop with the wine she had promised, the one in the green bottle that he liked, although thinking about it now, on the stairs, she was not sure whether he actually liked it or whether he had just said yes one time, three weeks ago, and she had built a whole theory around it.

She put her key in the lock and it occurred to her that she was nervous, which was, what, the fourth time? The fifth? Surely by now nervousness had to be a choice you were making. She was not sure she liked making it.

He was on the sofa with her book. The one she had been reading. He had not asked. She did not mind. She did not think she minded. She put the wine on the table.

He looked up and smiled the small private smile, the one that, she thought, was probably for her, although she could not actually verify this. He stood up.

She thought: oh. He was already crossing the room. She thought, here we go again. She thought, you sound like you do not want it. She thought, but I do.

0547. Safe house Charlie-Seven, kitchen.

The asset sat at the table in the chair facing the window. Reyes confirmed perimeter via the wall monitor — two units active, north and east — and crossed to the counter. He filled the kettle from the filtered tap. He set out two cups.

"How long," the asset said.

"Twelve hours. Then the transfer."

The asset nodded. She was wearing the shirt he had given her at 0231, after, when her own had been bagged for chemical processing. The shirt was three sizes too large. She had rolled the sleeves twice.

The kettle clicked off. He poured both cups. He set one in front of her and one across.

She did not lift hers immediately. She said:

"It will not be in the report."

"No."

"Not even in the operational notes."

"No."

He sat. He waited.

She said: "And you will not —"

"No."

She closed her eyes once. She opened them. She lifted the cup.
